title: Accellera’s FSL 1.0 Gives Functional Safety Data a Common Language
gist: Accellera approved Functional Safety Language (FSL) 1.0 on October 21, a Tcl-based common data model for exchanging FMEDA safety data across the IP-to-chip-to-system supply chain, supporting hierarchical FMEDAs and refinement of diagnostic coverage from fault-injection results. Nenni stresses it does not itself confer ISO 26262/IEC 61508 compliance and that value depends on tool-vendor adoption.

insights.claim: Functional safety data handoffs between IP suppliers, chipmakers and system manufacturers today rely on spreadsheets, proprietary databases and incompatible formats, and each conversion creates opportunities for omissions or misunderstandings.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Manual safety-data translation is a hidden cost and risk in automotive/industrial chip supply chains that standardization can remove.
insights.quote: every conversion creates an opportunity for omissions or misunderstandings

insights.claim: Accellera Systems Initiative approved Functional Safety Language Standard 1.0 for release on October 21, establishing a common language and data model for capturing and exchanging functional safety information, and it is available for download.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Creates a new interoperability layer that EDA and safety-tool vendors will need to support.

insights.claim: FSL 1.0 focuses on FMEDA, capturing failure modes, effects, safety mechanisms, technology information and safety requirements plus mappings to design representations, using Tcl-based syntax for machine processing.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Tcl syntax aligns with existing EDA scripting flows, easing integration into incumbent tools.

insights.claim: Support for hierarchical FMEDAs lets component analyses roll up into subsystem and system analyses, potentially reducing suppliers' repeated customer-specific deliverables and simplifying integrators' work while preserving traceability.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Lowers cost of selling safety-qualified IP into automotive, potentially benefiting IP vendors.

insights.claim: Reusing a component's safety analysis in a larger system does not automatically validate its assumptions about operating environment, implementation and use; engineering judgment is still required.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Standardized exchange does not eliminate integrator liability or safety engineering labor.
insights.quote: Moving that analysis into a larger system does not automatically establish that those assumptions remain valid.

insights.claim: FSL supports both assumption-based and design-mapped FMEDA and allows estimated diagnostic coverage to be refined with verification and fault-injection results, closing the gap between safety documentation and measured behavior.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Ties safety analysis to verification tools, creating a hook for fault-injection and verification vendors.

insights.claim: FSL supports calculation of safety failure-rate metrics associated with ISO 26262 and IEC 61508, but adopting it alone does not demonstrate compliance or certify a product.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Do not mistake FSL support claims by vendors for certification advantages.
insights.quote: adopting FSL alone does not demonstrate compliance or certify a product

insights.claim: FSL's value depends on adoption: tool vendors need compatible implementations, suppliers dependable export, and customers confidence imported data retains meaning, with round-trip exchange, hierarchical integration and post-change updates the key tests.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Watch for multi-vendor round-trip demos as the signal that the standard is gaining real traction.
insights.quote: Adoption will determine how much of that opportunity becomes routine practice.
